instances.brief: {{node_name}} (health: {{health}}%) crashed at 02:14 UTC. Support is reporting 503 errors.
instances.teaches: The line that explains a crash is rarely the last line in the log. The OOM kill precedes the downstream connection errors and restart noise that engineers read first.

given.context: Last 7 lines of the application worker log before the on-call alert fired.
given.output:
2026-09-18T02:14:31.003Z INFO  [app] Processing batch job: recommendation_refresh (batch_size=50000)
2026-09-18T02:14:31.487Z WARN  [app] Memory usage at 87%: 3.6 GB / 4.0 GB RSS
2026-09-18T02:14:32.001Z ERROR [kernel] Out of memory: Killed process 14782 (node) total-vm:4194304kB, anon-rss:3841024kB, file-rss:4096kB, shmem-rss:0kB
2026-09-18T02:14:32.010Z ERROR [supervisor] process 14782 exited with signal 9 (SIGKILL)
2026-09-18T02:14:33.221Z ERROR [nginx] upstream connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream
2026-09-18T02:14:34.107Z ERROR [nginx] upstream connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream
2026-09-18T02:14:35.890Z INFO  [supervisor] Restarting worker (node) attempt 1/3 — backoff 5s

solution.choice: Increase the container memory limit — the process is being killed by the Linux OOM killer

distractors.choice: Reconfigure nginx upstream settings — it is failing to connect to the backend
distractors.why_wrong: nginx is working correctly. It logged connection errors because the worker process was already dead. Reconfiguring nginx does nothing to address the memory exhaustion that killed the process.

distractors.choice: Disable the supervisor auto-restart to stop the restart loop
distractors.why_wrong: The supervisor is not causing the problem; it is attempting to recover from the OOM kill. Disabling restarts would leave the service permanently down while the root cause — memory exceeding the container limit — goes unfixed.

wrong_outcomes.shows: The worker is killed by the OOM killer again 47 seconds after restart. The same log sequence repeats: memory warning, kernel kill, nginx connection errors, supervisor restart.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The last two log lines are symptoms of the kill, not its cause. The memory limit was never changed.

instances.reveal: The diagnostic line is 'Out of memory: Killed process 14782 (node) ... anon-rss:3841024kB' — the Linux kernel OOM killer terminated the process after it consumed 3.75 GB of anonymous RSS against a 4 GB container limit. The two nginx 'Connection refused' errors and the supervisor restart that follow are consequences of the kill, not causes. Engineers who read logs from the bottom see a crashed process and a restart loop; engineers who read from the crash event see a memory exhaustion that will recur until the limit is raised or the allocation is reduced.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} is causing checkout slowness — p95 is 4.2s. The orders table is at 4.1M rows and growing.
instances.teaches: A range filter on an unindexed column forces the planner to read every row and discard most of them. An index on that column turns the scan into a seek.

given.context: This query runs on every checkout page load.
given.output:
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..89432.11 rows=4103922 width=84)
  Filter: (created_at > '2026-08-01'::date)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 3847291
  Planning Time: 0.112 ms
  Execution Time: 4118.442 ms

distractors.choice: CREATE INDEX ON orders(id)
distractors.why_wrong: id is already the primary key, and the filter never references it.

distractors.choice: Add a read replica and send this query to it
distractors.why_wrong: A replica runs the identical unindexed scan. You get another slow copy, not a fast one.

distractors.choice: Increase work_mem so the scan fits in memory
distractors.why_wrong: The cost is reading 4.1M rows, not sorting them. More memory does not reduce rows read.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Query still returns in 4.1s. The plan is unchanged — Seq Scan, 4.1M rows examined, 3.8M discarded.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Nothing you changed affects how the planner reaches those rows.

instances.reveal: The telling number is 'Rows Removed by Filter: 3847291' — the database read 4.1M rows to return roughly 250k. It does that because there is no ordered structure on created_at, so it cannot know where the range starts. An index on created_at lets it seek directly to 2026-08-01 and stop at the end, never touching the 3.8M rows it would otherwise discard.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} is causing invoice page timeouts under load. The order_items table has grown to 2.8M rows.
instances.teaches: A composite index only serves a range query if its leading column matches the filter. An index on (user_id, created_at) cannot accelerate a filter on created_at alone — the planner must scan the table regardless.

given.context: Average query time jumped from 80ms to 6.8s after table growth. A composite index (user_id, created_at) was added last quarter to speed up user-level queries.
given.output:
Seq Scan on order_items  (cost=0.00..128341.07 rows=2847919 width=72)
  Filter: (created_at > '2026-09-01 00:00:00+00')
  Rows Removed by Filter: 2642881
  Planning Time: 0.423 ms
  Execution Time: 6843.112 ms

distractors.choice: VACUUM ANALYZE order_items — stale statistics are preventing the planner from choosing the existing composite index
distractors.why_wrong: Statistics affect rowcount estimates but cannot make the planner use an index whose leading column is absent from the WHERE clause. The planner is correct not to use (user_id, created_at) when no user_id predicate exists.

distractors.choice: Rewrite the query to filter by user_id first so the composite index (user_id, created_at) can be used
distractors.why_wrong: The invoices page needs all recent invoices across all users. Adding a user_id constraint changes the query semantics entirely. The right fix is an index that fits the existing query, not a query rewritten to fit the existing index.

distractors.choice: Lower random_page_cost to 1.5 to encourage the planner to prefer index scans over sequential scans
distractors.why_wrong: Reducing random_page_cost makes index scans relatively cheaper, but the composite index still requires scanning its entire structure to find the right created_at range. The planner's choice is correct — the existing index offers minimal benefit for a filter on its non-leading column.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Query still returns in 6.8s. The EXPLAIN plan is unchanged — Seq Scan on order_items, 2.8M rows examined, 2.6M discarded.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Nothing you changed affects the planner's inability to use the (user_id, created_at) index for a filter on created_at alone.

instances.reveal: The Seq Scan appeared despite the composite index existing because the index leads with user_id, but the query has no predicate on user_id. A B-tree composite index can serve a range on its Nth column only if columns 1 through N-1 are equality-constrained. Since no user_id appears in the WHERE clause, the planner cannot use (user_id, created_at) efficiently. 'Rows Removed by Filter: 2642881' shows that 93% of examined rows were discarded — the same tell as the previous puzzle, but the fix is different: the existing index cannot be salvaged for this query shape; a new index with created_at as its leading column is needed.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} has had an elevated error rate for several hours. Nine deploys went out today.
instances.teaches: Correlate the error-rate inflection point with deploy timestamps, not with the most recent deploy. The most recent change is often innocent — it deployed into an already-broken environment.

given.context: Production deploy history for today. Error rate is the 5-minute average measured at deploy stabilisation.
given.output:
DEPLOY    DEPLOYED AT               COMMIT SUBJECT                                   ERROR RATE
g5h6i7j   2026-09-18 05:09 UTC     refactor: extract logger utility                 0.81%
c2d3e4f   2026-09-18 02:44 UTC     docs: add API documentation                      0.83%
y9z0a1b   2026-09-18 00:18 UTC     fix: add retry on cache miss                     0.81%
u6v7w8x   2026-09-17 21:33 UTC     chore: update deployment config                  0.79%
q3r4s5t   2026-09-17 19:07 UTC     feat: migrate cache layer to Redis               0.82%
m0n1o2p   2026-09-17 16:41 UTC     fix: handle null in profile view                 0.04%
i7j8k9l   2026-09-17 14:55 UTC     chore: bump axios to 1.7.4                       0.03%
e4f5g6h   2026-09-17 11:32 UTC     feat: add user export endpoint                   0.03%
a1b2c3d   2026-09-17 08:14 UTC     fix: update README typos                         0.02%

solution.choice: Revert q3r4s5t — the cache layer migration to Redis caused the error-rate inflection

distractors.choice: Revert g5h6i7j — it is the most recent deploy and error rates are currently elevated
distractors.why_wrong: g5h6i7j deployed at 05:09 into an environment already running at 0.81% error rate. Its subject is 'extract logger utility' — no cache or data-path logic changed. Reverting it would leave the same error rate that existed before it deployed.

distractors.choice: Revert y9z0a1b — it explicitly tried to fix cache misses, confirming the cache was broken before it shipped
distractors.why_wrong: y9z0a1b is a symptom response, not the cause. It deployed at 00:18 after the error rate had already been elevated since 19:07. Reverting it removes a band-aid but not the wound — the cache layer migration that broke the system remains.

distractors.choice: Revert u6v7w8x — deployment configuration changes frequently introduce environment-specific failures
distractors.why_wrong: u6v7w8x deployed at 21:33 when error rate was already 0.79% — elevated from the preceding deploy (q3r4s5t at 0.82%). u6v7w8x deployed into a broken environment; it did not create one.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Error rate remains at 0.81%. The revert did not affect the underlying cache connection failures introduced by the Redis migration.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The inflection is in the data: q3r4s5t at 19:07 is the first deploy with elevated error rates. Every deploy before it shows 0.02–0.04%; every deploy from it onward shows 0.79–0.83%.

instances.reveal: The inflection is in the ERROR RATE column: every deploy before 19:07 shows 0.02–0.04%, and every deploy from q3r4s5t onward shows 0.79–0.83%. q3r4s5t at 19:07 is the first deploy with elevated error rates, and the preceding deploy m0n1o2p at 16:41 still showed 0.04%. The subject confirms the mechanism: 'migrate cache layer to Redis' replaced the cache backend, and every request touching the cache has been failing since. g5h6i7j (the most recent deploy, 'refactor: extract logger utility') is innocent — it deployed into an already-broken environment at 0.81%.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} (Tier {{current_tier}}) has exhausted its database connection pool. The connection pool is at max and new requests are queuing. On-call paged 3 minutes ago.
instances.teaches: Connection leaks show up as 'too many connections' errors on the client, but the root cause is always a code path that acquires a connection and exits without releasing it — often inside an error handler that was never tested.

given.context: Application log from the API server, last 30 seconds before the alert.
given.output:
2026-09-19T14:21:44.001Z INFO  [db] Pool size: 48/50 connections active
2026-09-19T14:21:44.510Z WARN  [db] Pool size: 50/50 connections active — at max capacity
2026-09-19T14:21:45.002Z ERROR [db] could not get a connection from the pool — timeout after 5000ms
2026-09-19T14:21:45.003Z ERROR [api] /v2/orders [POST] 503 Service Unavailable — database unavailable
2026-09-19T14:21:45.110Z ERROR [db] could not get a connection from the pool — timeout after 5000ms
2026-09-19T14:21:46.200Z INFO  [db] Connection 0x7f44 returned to pool after 287s (expected: <2s)
2026-09-19T14:21:46.201Z WARN  [app] Long-running connection detected: 287 seconds — possible leak in order-processing handler

solution.choice: Fix the connection leak in the order-processing handler — a code path is not releasing its connection

distractors.choice: Increase the connection pool max size to 100
distractors.why_wrong: Doubling the pool size delays but does not fix the leak. The connection held for 287 seconds is not doing work — it is leaked. A larger pool will also exhaust if the leak rate is sustained.

distractors.choice: Restart the database to clear stale connections
distractors.why_wrong: Restarting the database drops all connections and causes a brief outage. The leak in the application code is untouched — connections will exhaust again within minutes.

wrong_outcomes.shows: The pool exhausts again 4 minutes later. The 287-second connection pattern reappears in the logs — the same order-processing path is still not releasing its connection on the error branch.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The fix treated the symptom (pool size or stale connections) without addressing the code path that holds a connection for 287 seconds and never returns it.

instances.reveal: The key line is 'Connection 0x7f44 returned to pool after 287s (expected: <2s)' followed by 'possible leak in order-processing handler'. A connection held for 4.7 minutes while the expected lease time is under 2 seconds means a code path acquired the connection and exited without releasing it — typically a missing finally block or an unhandled error path. The 503 errors are caused by the pool being full, not by a database problem.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} database load has spiked to 100% and p95 is 4.8s. On-call paged 90 seconds ago.
instances.teaches: A full cache flush under load triggers a stampede: every thread simultaneously misses the cache and hits the database at once. The root cause is the flush event, not the high database load that follows.

given.context: Application log from the API server, 30 seconds before the on-call alert fired.
given.output:
2026-09-19T10:14:40.001Z INFO  [cache] Cache flush requested for {{key_prefix}}:* (all keys)
2026-09-19T10:14:40.112Z INFO  [cache] Flushed 94,211 keys from {{node_name}}
2026-09-19T10:14:40.200Z WARN  [cache] Cache MISS: {{key_prefix}}:{{entity_id}}:preferences
2026-09-19T10:14:40.201Z WARN  [cache] Cache MISS: {{key_prefix}}:{{entity_id + 1}}:preferences
2026-09-19T10:14:40.202Z ERROR [cache] 18,400 concurrent cache misses — thundering herd on {{node_name}}
2026-09-19T10:14:40.410Z ERROR [db] connection pool exhausted — 50/50 connections active
2026-09-19T10:14:40.800Z ERROR [app] p95 latency: 4,820ms — database under load from cache miss storm

solution.choice: Cache stampede — a full flush of {{key_prefix}}:* evicted 94,211 keys simultaneously and 18,400 threads are now querying the database in parallel to rebuild them

distractors.choice: Database connection pool misconfigured — 50 connections is insufficient for normal traffic
distractors.why_wrong: The pool was adequate before the flush event. The exhaustion is a consequence of 18,400 simultaneous cache misses hammering the database at once, not a static pool ceiling misconfiguration.

distractors.choice: Cache server ran out of memory and evicted keys via LRU
distractors.why_wrong: The log shows an explicit flush request triggered by the operator, not an LRU eviction event. An LRU eviction removes keys gradually as memory fills; it would not produce 18,400 simultaneous misses in the same millisecond.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Connection pool doubled to 100. Load drops briefly then climbs again — every new cache miss still reaches the database. p95 stays at 4.3s for 14 minutes until the cache rewarms organically.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The pool exhaustion is a symptom of the stampede, not the cause. More connections give the database more simultaneous work to do, not less. The flush event is the root cause.

instances.reveal: The line 'Cache flush requested for {{key_prefix}}:* (all keys)' followed immediately by '18,400 concurrent cache misses — thundering herd' is the root cause. Every thread in the application simultaneously encountered a cold cache and fell through to the database, exhausting the connection pool within 200ms of the flush. The correct fix is to use scoped invalidation — {{key_prefix}}:{{entity_id}}:* instead of {{key_prefix}}:* — to evict only the updated entity rather than the entire key namespace.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} is causing checkout slowness — p95 is 8.1s. The query runs on every checkout page load for tenant {{tenant}}.
instances.teaches: Rows Removed by Filter shows exactly how wasteful a sequential scan is. An index on both filter columns turns the scan into a seek — only rows matching both tenant and date range are touched.

given.context: EXPLAIN ANALYZE output from the slow checkout query. The tenant_orders table has grown to 8.4M rows across all tenants.
given.output:
Seq Scan on tenant_orders  (cost=0.00..187432.11 rows=8401622 width=84)
  Filter: ((tenant_id = '{{tenant}}'::text) AND (created_at > '2026-09-01 00:00:00+00'))
  Rows Removed by Filter: 8219744
  Planning Time: 0.198 ms
  Execution Time: 8142.773 ms

distractors.choice: CREATE INDEX ON tenant_orders(tenant_id)
distractors.why_wrong: An index on tenant_id alone narrows to one tenant's rows but then performs a sequential scan across all their orders to find the date range. A composite index (tenant_id, created_at) lets the planner seek directly to the date boundary within the tenant's rows, skipping both the other tenants and the out-of-range dates.

distractors.choice: Add a read replica and route this query there
distractors.why_wrong: A replica runs the same unindexed sequential scan. Routing the query elsewhere gives you a separate slow copy, not a fast one. The fix requires an index, not a different host.

distractors.choice: Increase work_mem from 4MB to 256MB so the scan can hash into memory
distractors.why_wrong: The cost is reading 8.4M rows, not sorting or hashing them. More memory does not reduce the rows the planner must examine before applying the filter — only an index on the filter columns does that.

wrong_outcomes.shows: p95 still returns in 8.1s for tenant {{tenant}}. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the same Seq Scan on tenant_orders — 8.4M rows examined, 8.2M discarded by the filter.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Nothing you changed affects the planner's inability to skip rows that fail both the tenant_id and created_at predicates simultaneously.

instances.reveal: The tell is 'Rows Removed by Filter: 8219744' — the planner read 8.4M rows to return roughly 180k. A composite index on (tenant_id, created_at) lets the planner seek to the first row matching '{{tenant}}' and scan forward only to the date boundary, never touching other tenants or out-of-range dates. A single-column index on tenant_id helps but leaves a sequential pass across all of that tenant's orders for the date filter. An index on created_at alone does not help because the tenant_id equality predicate cannot use it — the planner needs the leading column to be the equality condition.

instances.brief: {{node_name}} CPU has been at 97% for 2 minutes. On-call paged 80 seconds ago.
instances.teaches: CPU thrash is caused by a specific runaway process, not by request load. The process id, command, and stack depth appear in the log before the downstream queue buildup that engineers tend to read first.

given.context: Last 8 lines of the application log before the on-call alert fired.
given.output:
2026-09-18T09:12:01.003Z INFO  [app] Health check OK (15ms)
2026-09-18T09:12:03.441Z INFO  [app] Cron job started: analytics_aggregation (pid={{pid}})
2026-09-18T09:12:04.220Z WARN  [app] CPU usage 71%
2026-09-18T09:12:05.881Z ERROR [app] CPU thrashing — recursive aggregation loop detected in pid {{pid}}, stack depth 847
2026-09-18T09:12:06.110Z WARN  [app] CPU usage 97%
2026-09-18T09:12:07.003Z INFO  [app] GC paused for 820ms
2026-09-18T09:12:08.551Z WARN  [app] 42 requests queued behind CPU lock
2026-09-18T09:12:09.000Z INFO  [app] Thread pool exhausted

solution.choice: Kill pid {{pid}} — the analytics_aggregation cron job entered an infinite recursive loop

distractors.choice: Tune GC settings — 820ms GC pauses are degrading throughput
distractors.why_wrong: The GC pause is a consequence of CPU saturation, not its cause. Tuning GC parameters will not stop the recursive loop that is consuming all available CPU cycles.

distractors.choice: Scale up the thread pool — 42 queued requests indicate the pool is undersized
distractors.why_wrong: The requests are queued because the CPU is saturated by a single process, not because thread count is low. Adding threads gives them more workers competing for the same saturated CPU.

wrong_outcomes.shows: GC tuning applied. CPU stays at 97%. The recursive loop in pid {{pid}} continues consuming all available cycles. 4 minutes later the process runs out of stack space and crashes, taking the node down entirely.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The line 'recursive aggregation loop detected in pid {{pid}}, stack depth 847' names both the cause and the process. GC tuning and thread scaling address downstream symptoms, not the runaway process itself.

instances.reveal: The line 'CPU thrashing — recursive aggregation loop detected in pid {{pid}}, stack depth 847' identifies both the cause (a recursive loop with no base case) and the process (analytics_aggregation at pid {{pid}}). The GC pause at 820ms, the 42 queued requests, and the thread pool exhaustion all appear after the CPU is already saturated — they are consequences, not causes. Engineers who read logs bottom-up see congestion; engineers who read from the cron-job start event see a loop that can be killed immediately with `kill -9 {{pid}}`.
